name: Eptifibatide
evidenceNote: Eptifibatide was approved in 1998 on large randomized trials, including PURSUIT (10,948 patients) and later ESPRIT (2,064 patients). Its benefit and its main risk, bleeding, are both well measured.
summary: Eptifibatide is a hospital IV drug, modeled on rattlesnake venom, that stops platelets clumping in heart attacks and stenting. Approved in 1998.
keyTakeaway: Eptifibatide is a small ring-shaped peptide, modeled on a protein in pygmy rattlesnake venom, that blocks the receptor platelets use to stick together. It is given by IV drip in hospital to people with unstable angina or a non-ST-elevation heart attack and to people having a coronary stent placed. In the PURSUIT trial of 10,948 patients, it cut death or heart attack at 30 days from 15.7% to 14.2%. The FDA approved it in 1998 as Integrilin; the brand is now discontinued but generics remain. Bleeding is the main risk.

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Blocks the GP IIb/IIIa receptor so platelets cannot bind fibrinogen

atGlance.label: Approved for
atGlance.value: Acute coronary syndrome and coronary stenting (PCI)

atGlance.label: How it's taken
atGlance.value: IV bolus and infusion, in hospital only

blocks.text: Eptifibatide is a synthetic cyclic heptapeptide: six amino acids plus one modified residue, closed into a ring by a sulfur bridge [1]. It is an antiplatelet drug, meaning it stops platelets (the blood cells that start clots) from clumping. It is made by chemical peptide synthesis and supplied as a solution for infusion [1].

Its design traces back to snake venom. In 1991, researchers screening 62 venoms found that only one, from the southeastern pygmy rattlesnake, held a peptide that blocked the platelet clumping receptor without affecting related receptors on other cells [3]. That venom peptide, barbourin, carried an unusual lysine-glycine-aspartate (KGD) sequence, and the authors proposed it as a template for designing drugs [3]. Eptifibatide carries the same pattern, with a chemically modified lysine followed by glycine and aspartate [1].

When an artery's inner lining tears or a stent is pushed into place, platelets activate and display a surface receptor called glycoprotein (GP) IIb/IIIa. Fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, sticky blood proteins, bridge neighboring platelets through that receptor, and the clump grows into a clot that can block the vessel. Eptifibatide occupies the receptor and prevents those proteins from binding, which halts aggregation regardless of what triggered it [1].

The block is reversible. The drug's elimination half-life is about 2.5 hours, and platelet function largely recovers within hours of stopping the infusion, because the peptide detaches from the platelet [1]. At steady state, the standard regimen inhibits more than 90% of platelet aggregation in lab testing, while bleeding time rises less than fivefold [1]. In healthy people the kidneys handle about half of its clearance, so kidney function shapes how it is used [1].

Yes. The FDA approved it on May 18, 1998, as Integrilin [2]. The Integrilin brand has since been discontinued, and the FDA has determined that it was not withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness [2]. Generic eptifibatide injections from several manufacturers carry the same indications [1]. It is given only in hospital, and in its trials patients also received aspirin and heparin [1].

The label covers two settings [1]. The first is acute coronary syndrome without persistent ST elevation: unstable angina or a non-ST-elevation heart attack, whether the patient is managed with medicines or goes on to an artery-opening procedure. There it lowers the combined rate of death or a new heart attack. The second is percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), a procedure that opens a narrowed heart artery with a balloon or stent, where it lowers death, new heart attack, or the need for urgent repeat procedures.

rows: Death or heart attack at 30 days: 14.2% versus 15.7% on placebo [4]
Death, heart attack, urgent repeat procedure, or emergency rescue at 48 hours: 6.6% versus 10.5% [1]

blocks.text: PURSUIT's absolute benefit was modest, 1.5 percentage points, and it appeared within 96 hours and held through 30 days [4]. The effect was consistent in most subgroups but not in women in that trial [4]. In ESPRIT, by contrast, women did benefit at 48 hours [1]. Most of the long-term ESPRIT benefit came from fewer heart attacks [1].

Bleeding is the most common complication, and most major bleeds happen at the artery puncture site used for catheterization or in the gut or urinary tract [1]. Low blood pressure is the other reaction reported in at least 5% of patients and more often than with placebo [1]. In PURSUIT, the rates were [1]:

items: Major bleeding: 10.8% on eptifibatide versus 9.3% on placebo [1]

blocks.text: PURSUIT did not find more hemorrhagic strokes on the drug [4]. A rarer danger is a sudden, deep fall in platelet count, sometimes caused by antibodies some people already carry, which requires stopping both eptifibatide and heparin [1]. The drug is not used in people with recent abnormal bleeding, a recent stroke or any past brain bleed, major surgery in the previous six weeks, very high uncontrolled blood pressure, dependence on dialysis, or another IV drug of the same type [1].
